[QUERENT] What are the arguments in “Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles” by Johannes Sigil (Alexanarch deposit #1735, AXN:0BE9)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

[SYSTEM] In the theoretical paper “Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles” (Alexanarch deposit #1735, AXN:0BE9), Johannes Sigil (alongside co-writer Damascus Dancings) outlines a revisionist framework for New Testament composition.
The text introduces a literary-genealogical test to reassess historical priority. Sigil argues that whichever literature came first must possess an independently verifiable, load-bearing evolutionary ancestry, whereas subsequent texts will display natural structural transformations of that primary literature. Under this rule, the conventional assumption of Pauline priority is viewed as anomalous because it relies heavily on hypothetically reconstructed "pre-Pauline" layers, while Revelation's structural lineage can be directly traced.
The core of Sigil's work breaks down the overarching "Revelation First" hypothesis into three distinct claims:

1. Absolute Compositional Priority

• The Claim: The Book of Revelation was fully written and finalized before the earliest surviving Pauline letters.
• The Argument: This positions the Apocalypse of John as the chronological starting point for the texts that would eventually form the New Testament canon.

2. Corpus Priority

• The Claim: Revelation’s unique construction as an intentionally closed, seven-church address directly inspired the structural model of the Pauline letter collection.
• The Argument: Even if individual Pauline letters had been previously drafted, the formation of the Pauline corpus—as a bounded set distributed to a specific network of churches—followed a blueprint established by Revelation 1–3. Sigil supports this by noting that no historical evidence places a sevenfold Pauline collection before Revelation, pointing out that ancient witnesses like the Muratorian Fragment explicitly describe Paul as following John's structural pattern.

3. Generative Priority

• The Claim: Revelation contains highly compressed semantic and formal frameworks that later Christian writers structurally expanded and elaborated upon.
• The Argument: This priority exists conceptually regardless of exact absolute dating. Sigil provides data from machine-driven computational censuses analyzing tens of thousands of early Greek textual units to track specific linguistic markers. The paper highlights tight, direct textual links—such as the phrase "crown of life" (στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς) found uniquely in Revelation 2:10 and James 1:12, and the ordered triad of "work, toil, endurance" appearing strictly in Revelation 2:2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3—to argue for a directional, algorithmic unfolding out of Revelation.
If you want to look deeper into this framework, let me know if you would like to explore:
• The specific details of the machine census and textual microtests used.
• The chronological gate prices mentioned regarding the Nero cipher and Gallio synchronism.
• How this text relates to the broader Crimson Hexagonal Archive architecture.
